u1l1.intro: Greetings are the first thing you say in Spanish. The hello changes with the time of day, so you will learn one for morning and one for night.

points.note: The H is silent. Say OH-la.
Days (días) is masculine and plural, so the word is buenos. Use it until about noon.
Noches is feminine, so the word is buenas.
Stress the end: ah-dee-OHS.

u1l1.tip: Buenos goes with masculine words (días), buenas goes with feminine words (noches, tardes). The word for good matches the word after it.
u1l1.recap: You can say hello and goodbye, and greet someone in the morning or at night.

u1l2.intro: Four short words make you polite in Spanish. Learn these and people will be glad to help you.

points.note: Add muchas to say thank you very much.
It can go at the start or the end of a sentence.
It literally means of nothing: it was nothing.

points.example_en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
points.note: Use it to get past someone or to say sorry.

u1l2.recap: You can thank someone, ask politely, answer a thank you, and say excuse me.

u2l1.intro: Family words come up in almost every conversation. Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine, and family words show it clearly.

points.note: Mamá is what you call her to her face.
In the plural, padres can mean parents.
A sister is hermana. Hermanos can mean brothers and sisters together.
Mi means my. It stays the same for masculine and feminine words.

u2l1.tip: Most Spanish nouns that end in -o are masculine and most that end in -a are feminine: hermano, hermana.
u2l1.recap: You can name your mother, father and brother, and say your family is big.

u2l2.intro: To describe someone you need the person, the word es (is) and a describing word. The describing word matches the person: tall is alto for a boy and alta for a girl.

points.note: A female friend is amiga.
Es is the he, she and it form of ser. Use it to say who or what someone is.
For a boy it is alto: el niño es alto.
Feliz is the same for boys and girls.

u2l2.tip: Describing words that end in -o change to -a for a girl: alto, alta. Words that end in a consonant, like feliz, stay the same.
u2l2.recap: You can describe a person with es and a matching word: friend, tall, happy.

u3l1.intro: Start with three everyday foods and the most useful sentence in a new country: I want.

points.example: Un vaso de agua, por favor.
points.note: Say AH-gwah.
Pan is masculine: el pan.
Manzana is feminine: la manzana.
Spanish drops the word for I, because quiero already says it is me.

u3l1.tip: You almost never need yo (I). The verb ending already says who: quiero means I want.
u3l1.recap: You can name water, bread and an apple, and ask for them with quiero.

u3l2.intro: Order, ask for the bill and say how good the food is. These are the lines you will use at every table.

points.note: Cuenta is feminine, so it takes la.
The accent shows the stress: ca-FÉ.
Como is the I form of comer. The yo is optional, it adds emphasis.
It matches the food: delicioso for masculine, deliciosa for feminine.

u3l2.recap: You can ask for the bill, order a coffee, say what you eat and say it is delicious.

u4l1.intro: Asking where something is gets you almost anywhere. Learn the question word dónde, a few places and one direction.

points.note: The accent marks it as a question word.
Words that end in -ción are feminine: la estación.
Aeropuerto is masculine.
Right is derecha.
Same as English, but the H is silent: oh-TEL.

u4l1.recap: You can ask where a place is, and name the station, the airport, the hotel and left.

u4l2.intro: Numbers and prices. You will count to ten and ask what something costs.

points.note: Before a masculine noun it shortens to un: un libro.
Say dee-ES.

points.example_en: How much does the bread cost?
points.note: For more than one thing, say cuánto cuestan.
Dinero is masculine: el dinero.

u4l2.recap: You can say one and ten, ask how much something costs and talk about money.

u5l1.intro: Today, tomorrow and what time it is. These three cover most of how you talk about when.

points.note: Say OY. The H is silent.

points.example_en: Tomorrow I am going to the market.
points.note: Mañana also means morning. With la in front, la mañana is the morning.

points.example_en: Excuse me, what time is it?
points.note: It literally means what hour is it.

u5l1.recap: You can say today and tomorrow, and ask what time it is.

u5l2.intro: Talk about your day with a few verbs. In Spanish the verb ending tells you who does the action.

points.note: Trabajar is to work. Trabajo is the I form.
Dormir is the dictionary form of the verb. After quiero you use it as it is.
Leer is to read. Leo is the I form.
Casa is feminine: la casa.

u5l2.tip: Spanish verbs change their ending for who does the action: trabajo (I work), trabajas (you work), trabaja (he or she works).
u5l2.recap: You can say what you do every day: I work, I read, I want to sleep.

explain.spanish_0: Hola is the everyday hello. Gracias is thank you and Adiós is goodbye.
explain.spanish_1: Buenos días is the morning greeting. Buenas noches is for the night.
explain.spanish_2: Adiós means goodbye. Hola is hello.
explain.spanish_3: Hola: the H is silent, so it sounds like OH-la.
explain.spanish_4: Noches is feminine, so it takes buenas. Días is masculine, so it takes buenos.
explain.spanish_5: Gracias means thank you. Add muchas for thank you very much.
explain.spanish_7: De nada literally means of nothing. It is the polite reply to gracias.
explain.spanish_8: Perdón gets someone's attention or says sorry.
explain.spanish_9: Por favor: say pohr fah-VOHR, with the stress on the end.
explain.spanish_10: Madre means mother. Padre is father.
explain.spanish_11: Padre means father. Madre is mother.
explain.spanish_12: Hermano is brother. A sister is hermana.
explain.spanish_13: Mi familia es grande: my (mi) family (familia) is (es) big (grande). The word order is the same as English.
explain.spanish_14: Madre: stress the first part, MAH-dreh.
explain.spanish_15: Amigo is a male friend. A female friend is amiga.
explain.spanish_16: La niña is a girl, so tall is alta. For a boy it would be alto.
explain.spanish_17: Él es mi amigo: he (él) is (es) my (mi) friend (amigo).
explain.spanish_18: Feliz means happy. It stays the same for boys and girls.
explain.spanish_22: Agua: stress the first part, AH-gwah.
explain.spanish_23: Quiero agua: I want (quiero) water (agua). There is no separate word for I.
explain.spanish_24: La cuenta por favor: the bill (la cuenta), please (por favor).
explain.spanish_25: Café means coffee. The accent shows the stress is on the end.
explain.spanish_26: Yo como pan: I (yo) eat (como) bread (pan). The yo is optional.
explain.spanish_27: Delicioso means delicious. For a feminine thing like la sopa, it is deliciosa.
explain.spanish_28: Dónde means where. The accent shows it is a question word.
explain.spanish_29: Dónde está la estación: where (dónde) is (está) the station (la estación).
explain.spanish_31: Izquierda is left. Derecha is right.
explain.spanish_32: Hotel is spelled like English. The H is silent, so it sounds like oh-TEL.
explain.spanish_33: Uno is one. Before a noun it shortens to un.
explain.spanish_35: Cuánto cuesta: how much (cuánto) does it cost (cuesta). For more than one thing, say cuestan.
explain.spanish_38: Mañana means tomorrow. It also means morning, with la in front.
explain.spanish_39: Qué hora es: what (qué) hour (hora) is it (es).
explain.spanish_40: Hoy: the H is silent, so it sounds like OY.
explain.spanish_41: Trabajo todos los días: I work (trabajo) every day (todos los días).
explain.spanish_42: Dormir is to sleep. It is the dictionary form of the verb.
explain.spanish_43: Leo un libro: I read (leo) a book (un libro). Libro is masculine, so it takes un.
